utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Judge Mindua is again not available today. The Chamber decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis on with two Judges this morning. Could the next -- is the next witness ready, then? In that case, he could be brought in. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour. This witness will be testifying in Dutch, and it's my understanding the Dutch interpreter, who's in one of the booths, will be listening in English and translating the English to Dutch and back again, so it may take a little while -- a little longer than we're used to. But we'll try to go slow, so it shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he will be a 92 ter witness, and I won't spend too much time with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. It's not the first time that you're here as a witness, so I think you know the procedure very well. Could you please read aloud the affirmation which is shown to you now on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. McCloskey has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First, can you give us your name, and spell it for the court reporter, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Paul Groenewegen, which is spelled P-a-u-l, Groenewegen, G-r-o-e-n-e-w-e-g-e-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is it fair to say you understand English pretty well, but that speaking, you much prefer to speak Dutch, and you speak -- sorry, I'll just leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you do recall testifying here in July 1996 at the Rule 61 hearing, July 2003 at the Blagojevic trial, and October 2006 in the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you were asked questions on this case, would your answers be the same as they were before?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I am going to read a brief summary soon. We would like to mark the Popovic testimony as the -- excuse me, the Blagojevic testimony as the 92 ter statement; that is, R6206. And I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the number. I think it is recorded not correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: R number is 6206.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is the testimony of the Blagojevic case. Yes. That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P98, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I will read a brief summary now. Mr. Groenewegen enlisted in the Dutch Army in January 1994, when he was 17 years old. He was sent to Bosnia with the Dutch Army and served there from January through July 1995. At the time, he was a private assigned to Charlie Company based in Potocari, with assignments to OP rotations at OP Mike and OP November. In early July 1995, Mr. Groenewegen was stationed at OP Mike. During this time, Bosnian Serb forces were shooting towards the OP with small-calibre and large-calibre weapons and mortars. He learned that the other OPs were also coming under fire at that time. He left OP Mike and returned to Potocari on 10 July. On 11 July, he was on duty in Potocari when Muslim refugees came into Potocari, and he described them as exhausted and full of fear. That day, the base filled up with Muslim refugees, and after that, the refugees sought shelter in nearby factories. On 12 July, the Bosnian Serb Army entered Potocari. At the time the soldiers were coming into Potocari, Mr. Groenewegen heard shells exploding and saw houses catching fire. That day, he and his Dutch colleagues were tasked with keeping the Bosnian Serb Army and the refugees apart. That same day, buses arrived. The first people to go there were those who wanted to get into the buses on their own account. The people who didn't want to get in withdrew into the background and were forced afterwards to get into those buses. For the Muslims who were unwilling to get on the buses, initially there was only shouting and people were being called names, and if they still didn't want to get in, then violence was used by the Serb soldiers. Also, men were selected from the crowd of Muslims and gathered in an empty house by Serb soldiers. When the house was full, the men were taken away in buses. The transportation of the Muslim population continued until the evening and then it stopped. On the next day, 13 July, Mr. Groenewegen had the same duties he had the day before. Men continued to be separated that day. At one point, his attention was drawn to shouting, and he saw a man from the crowd dressed in civilian clothes on the road, who was being handled aggressively by some Serb soldiers. About 10 or 15 minutes after seeing this, Mr. Groenewegen's attention was drawn again to this same man. This time, from about 30 metres away, he saw the man placed up against the wall of a nearby house by Serb soldiers. He saw a Serb soldier shoot the man through the head from a distance of about three metres. The man collapsed after being shot, and the Serb soldiers walked away. Mr. Groenewegen noticed other Serb soldiers look to the area of the shooting after that shot was fired, but they just continued their activities. That finishes my brief summary. I have just a few clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. McCloskey, there is a problem of wording. Several times, you used the word "Serb soldiers." I think you should clarify it, that they were soldiers of the Bosnian Serb Army and not of the Serb Army. We had the same problem yesterday as well. You realised that later that day. Are you sure that you mean Serb soldiers or Bosnian Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe that's a reflection of the previous statements where the witnesses tend to call them Serb soldiers. That's what it should be, though I also recall that many of the Dutch referred to the soldiers as BSA, which means Bosnian Serb Army. So I will clarify that with the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we clear up this issue? In my summary, I said "Serb soldiers." Can you clarify for that? How did you refer normally -- that you and the Dutch refer to the soldiers that were there in Potocari? Who were they to you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: For me, those were the people who came from outside the enclave, and there was no unity in the uniform, they had many camouflage-type uniforms. But we felt that they were Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did many times the DutchBat refer to them as the BSA?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was often used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your mind, what did that mean? What did that stand for in English?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: For us, "BSA" represented the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And could we go into private session for one short moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were in Potocari on that first day, 12 July, you have described the crowd of Muslims being full of fear. Can you tell the Judges, you know, what you saw that made you come to that conclusion? How did you know that they were full of fear?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: These people were really trying very hard to reach the Potocari compound, and it was clear to us that these people were not at their ease. We could easily say that they were really fearful, full of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've described the first group trying to get on the buses and another group that wasn't. Can you describe the situation in just a little more detail for the Judges? And first the group that was trying to get on the buses, what did they look like? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As from the moment the buses arrived, well, of course, we couldn't hear all the conversations which these people had. But as far as I gathered, these people were given the choice to board the buses themselves, and many of them did it in the first stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did they do it? Was it just -- can you describe the situation? Was it calm and orderly?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I had the impression these people were really eager to board the bus and they were really eager to leave that place as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about this other group you described? What were they doing, the ones that didn't seem so eager?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: These people were trying to hide and to withdraw to the back of the group, and finally they were all forced to board the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe this force?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: At first, people were only -- were only yelling at them, but then they -- people were being threatened with weapons. And when they didn't move, then they were really forced physically to board the buses and go towards the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "forced physically," can you tell us -- give us some kind of an idea what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, it was mainly that people were being grabbed and they were being drawn, and people were being kicked and given, you know, the -- they were being hit so that they would move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go briefly to the shooting you witnessed. The victim of this shooting, where was this person? Could you tell whether this was a Bosnian Serb, or a Muslim, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I saw, it was a person who was taken from the main group, but I can't tell what his origin was. I can't say that with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "the main group," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The main group of refugees who had gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us a rough idea of the age of the person, the man that you saw taken from the group?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I think he might have been in his 30s, early 40s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the person that shot him, what was that person wearing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It was a camouflage dress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think the rest of it is laid out in your testimony. So you have, over the years, seen an aerial image of this scene and made markings about where the house was and where the person was shot, and so -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know it's been a long time, but let's see if we can do that one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have a -- number 950 is our number for this photograph. This is an unmarked version, and I would -- and if we could blow that up. Keep going, if we could. Can we go one more? We need the white -- that bright white house -- perfect. Right there, right there, that's fine. And could you blow it up one more time? Can you concentrate on that photo? Could we go back again? Actually, that's okay. If we could put that building in the bottom a bit, a little bit farther in the bottom. Okay. Right there is -- do you want us to go back or can you make this photo out?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I think one step down, it would be somewhat more defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could go back one more time, we'll get a little less pixels. One more. It's perfect, but we just need one more zoom. Zoom in a bit more, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that clear for you? I know this is difficult sometimes. Do you see the area where you saw the man get shot?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I recognise the photograph well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you take that marker and put a dot where you saw the man get shot?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that red mark. And can you put an X roughly where the man -- well, where the man was that shot him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't quite make that out as an X, so they look the same to me. So make that a little bigger X, if you could.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And a G if you recall about where you were when you saw this.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, I think that will do it. Thank you. I have nothing further, Mr. President, and I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The marked photograph will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P99, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, now the accused, Mr. Tolimir, has the right to cross-examine you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace be with this institution and everybody following these proceedings. God willing, these proceedings will be finished soon and happily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I am -- you are not a protected witness. I'll call you by your name. I'm going to read some questions to you, and I'm going to put questions to you. And every time I put a question to you or quote back your testimony to you, or a new question, I will say, Thank you, and then I will ask you to please start answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, in this case, especially today, it is necessary to speak very slowly because we have additional interpretation from English -- from B/C/S to Dutch, and therefore you need to pause and to read especially very slowly. Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, how old were you when you joined the Dutch Army? That would be my first question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I was 17 years old. I was 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You testified in the Popovic case, and you said that you joined the army in 1994 and that you arrived in Srebrenica as a member of the DutchBat of UNPROFOR. Tell me, where did you serve from January 1994 until July 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: At first, from January 1994, I served in Assen. And in January 1995, we left for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then say, for the transcript, that in 1995, in January, you arrived in Srebrenica, that you didn't arrive there in 1994?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: 1994 is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groenewegen, before you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you have to undergo training to become a member of UNPROFOR? And if you did, what was the training about?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. It's the standard training for us to be prepared for deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. How old do you have to be in the Netherlands to apply to serve as a professional in the army? In other words, when do you qualify to become a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can tell you about my personal experience. I was one of the last people required to serve in the military, and opted to be a professional -- opted for a career in the military. I was one of the final conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. Are you saying that you were a minor when you joined your battalion and UNPROFOR in January 1995?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Negative, because I was 18 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you were recruited or enlisted in the Dutch military, were you a minor then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: When I received my summons, I was 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. Just for the record, could you please tell us, were you a minor in 1994, when you joined the DutchBat of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I was 17 when I registered to join the army, but not when I became part of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You left the military in 2003; am I right in saying that? And if I am right, could you please tell us why you left the army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: To be specific, that was in 2004. The reason was that 10 years was enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think if you raise this question, we should go into private session, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have a redaction, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, could you please look at 1D72, which is now on the screen. This is your statement provided 29 September 1986 -- I apologise. 1995. Thank you. Do you see that document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groenewegen, this statement that we see on the screen does not have the form of a classical statement. I would like to ask you the following: Who was it who provided this statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise. My question was wrong, I misspoke. That's why I'm going to repeat it. I meant to ask you: Who took your statement, which does not have the form of a classical statement? In my previous question, I asked you who it was who provided the statement. I meant to ask you who it was you provided the statement to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The name of that individual is listed at the bottom as the interviewer, and that is Peter Cornelis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us who that person was affiliated to at that time, which institution that person worked for at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, for the sake of the record, you should mention -- you should state that the full name of this person is Peter Cornelis Stephanus Staal, and I think the family name is Staal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as we know, the witness does understand English. This is also -- I believe the original is in Dutch, as we can -- may be able to tell, because there should be a signature. So I don't know how much detail he's going into it, but it would be a courtesy to the witness. I'm sorry, I may be mistaken on that. So if we find the Dutch, we'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to know who the statement was provided to and what was that person's capacity. I just needed to know that in order to understand whether that person, who took the statement, could appreciate the witness's statement fully, whether he was familiar with the situation that the witness was testifying about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: However, I'm sorry, I did not receive an answer. Could I please be given an answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question one more time so I know exactly what you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I want to know, the statement that you provided on the 29th September 1995, which is before you on the screen, was it provided to an official who was a member of the police, the military, the judiciary in Holland? Thank you. And where were you at the time when you provided your statement on the 29th September 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was at the barracks, Johan Willem Friso Barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was the person Mr. Staal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, it was somebody from the Koninklijke Marechaussee, the military police, the Dutch military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just briefly, that policeman from the Dutch military police, did he inform you that you were providing that statement for the purpose of the Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and that that statement could be used there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No reference was made to it at that time. I wasn't told that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please also tell us, before you went to Srebrenica, before you were deployed there, did you know anything about Srebrenica, about the ratio of forces in the battle-field, who was involved in combat there? Were you explained what the mandate of the United Nations was in Srebrenica and also what the mandate of your unit was before you were deployed in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the multifaceted -- that's a very complex-faceted question, which if it can be asked in parts, I think it's fair, but that -- it's impossible to answer a question like that in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not fully in agreement with you, Mr. McCloskey. He asked if this witness knew anything about Srebrenica. It was a question not about the facts, but if he was told about the facts, and what was his knowledge at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my -- that, of course, is a very big question about perhaps the history of the peoples, and then he got specific in the same question and asked about the UN mandate, which is very specific and potentially very different than the history of Srebrenica, what he knows about it. So if he wants -- the answer, we won't know if it's history that he's learned about or the mandate. We won't know from his answer, unless we try to clarify that. That was my only point. Fair questions. There's a difference, in my view, between the mandate that his forces had and what he knew about Srebrenica before he went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, that was not the question: "Were you explained what the mandate of the United Nations was in Srebrenica?" "Were you explained," this was the question for the witness, and I think this is the right of the accused to ask this question. Could you tell us what you were told at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During a training period, we were reasonably informed of the situation and the situation -- the geographical situation, the various parties, and of course we also received the mandate of the United Nations, and we were informed of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, when you testified in the Blagojevic and Jokic case, on page 1015, to the Prosecutor's question about your duties and tasks in Srebrenica between January and July 1995, you answered that you mostly went on patrols. And then on page 1016, when you were asked what the purpose of the patrolling was, your answer was whether the two warring sides were engaged in any conflicts and whether a cease-fire was being observed. Do you remember those two questions, and do you remember your answers to them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I remember the questions. I don't exactly remember what I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. I just wanted to jog your memory about that trial. And now please answer this: Did you testify -- or did you provide a statement to the Ministry of Defence when the Ministry of Defence carried out an investigation among your fellow soldiers about the events in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm re-reading the question. At the time, we were asked questions by the Ministry of Defence about our stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. I would like to present a report compiled by the Ministry of Defence. The document number is 1D71. Could the Court please produce document 1D71. I would like to ask the witness whether he was familiar with the report and the findings of the Dutch government with regard to the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I am aware of the document, but I don't know its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the transcript, do you know that on the 4th of October, 1995, in Assen, this report by the Ministry of Defence was published, it was based on the statements of Dutch soldiers and officers who were part of the mission in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The fact that it was the 4th of October, 1995, that's quite possible. But the rest, yes, the rest is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you agree with the fact -- or, rather, was your statement enclosed or was it taken into account when the Ministry of Defence published this report? Did they take your statement into account when they compiled the report and then published it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, I'm aware of the document. But I've never read it, personally, so I really can't say more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the transcript, can we then state that you've not had an occasion to familiarise yourself with this document, produced by the Ministry of Defence, as a report about the events that took place in Srebrenica in 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It's not the fact that I didn't have the opportunity, but the fact that I did not want to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have not read this report, I'm going to quote some of the things from this document which are of some relevance for the cross-examination. As a matter of fact, I'm just going to jog your memory about some things. You said that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 10 of the document, in paragraph 2.23, which is also page 10 in English and page 13 in the Serbian, could this please be shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A reference is made about the mandate of the UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, and it says as follows, and I quote from paragraph 2.23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you can pause a little bit and wait for the moment it will appear on the screen. It is helpful for the interpreters and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If you agree, I will move on with my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will now read out point 2.23 : "The DutchBat was entrusted with the following tasks based on the above-mentioned agreement on the cease-fire and resolution." In other words, this is part of the agreement between the Government of the Netherlands. Under 2.23(a): "To monitor compliance with the ceasefire." "(b) To disarm the BiH." And: "(c) To support the provisions of humanitarian aid." I should also explain to you, Mr. Groenewegen, that we're only going to be discussing here the mandate as described under (b), in other words, to disarm the BiH, because it is stated here that that was within your mandate. Could you please now answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? It was not recorded because of interpretation problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, could you please tell us what measures were taken in Srebrenica in order to disarm BiH members? That will be my question, and of course I expect to give -- I expect you to give us your view, as a private.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I can give you is my position as a soldier. During that semester we carried out patrols regularly, and it was only on three or four occasions that we encountered BiH members with weapons or in training. And insofar as we tried to do anything, it was very hard to do anything because there were dangers of minefields. And these people, we couldn't find them. When we attempted to find them, it was very hard to locate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. Just tell us now, in the course of your patrols and in those missions, how far were you from positions of the BH Army, or members of the BH Army, or the positions of the 28th Division that was located in Srebrenica and its surroundings? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I suppose you mean the people we saw carrying weapons around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify. Did you have to send the report on where units of the BH Army were deployed in the territory that you were keeping under control and whether they were complying with the agreement on the cease-fire? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: In my personal experience, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. Can you please just tell us, did you personally take part in the patrols, and were there any instances where your patrol, of which you were a member, actually disarmed a member of the BH Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I was never present during patrols where people were being disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, since you were monitoring the implementation of the cease-fire and disarming, did you ever get information from your colleagues or from those who assigned you to tasks that members of the BH Army left or went out of the demilitarised zone, and that from outside the demilitarised zone they would actually take certain actions?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: During the six months we stayed there, I was never being told anything of the sort. I only heard such things after I had returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. If you allow me, I would like to read a statement by your commander, the DutchBat Battalion, Thomas Karremans, who assigned tasks to all of you. I will quote his words in Blagojevic/Jokic case on page 11165 [as interpreted] of the transcript. Thank you. Thomas Karremans, in his testimony in the Blagojevic/Jokic case, on page 1165 of the transcript, stated the following, I quote: "From time to time, Muslim fighters would leave the enclave and return on the same night. Sometimes we could hear shooting outside the enclave, and usually a day or two later we would be informed by the other side that something had happened, that there had been an incident." My question is this: Did you ever take part in any action in order to try to prevent BH Army members to leave the demilitarised zone and then to launch attacks from outside the zone against the Serb civilian population and Serb soldiers around Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I never took part in such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether any such actions were ever taken? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the soldiers in your unit or your complement ever receive any information from your superior command, or from the civilians, or from the other side, on Muslim Army activities outside the safe area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I have heard things said about it, but on very rare occasions. But we never got any official information from our official sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. Do you remember, by any chance, why a conflict erupted on the eve of the fall of Srebrenica at the check-point in the Zeleni Jadar area, and was that close to the observation post where you served? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that because I don't know the name Zeleni Jadar. It doesn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that the BH Army in Srebrenica, as early as January 1995, forbade members of the DutchBat to patrol in the area known under the name of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the name. Could the accused please repeat it? Interpreter's note: Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the area known as the Bandera Triangle. Thank you. The name is Bandera Triangle, and I asked the witness whether he knew that the Muslims had forbidden the DutchBat to patrol that area called or known under the name of Bandera Triangle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: If that was truly the case, if it was forbidden, I was never informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness now be shown document 1D71, page 15, 15, paragraph 2.40. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the right page number is 14 instead of 15, but we have paragraph 2.40 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. All that matters is that we actually have that very paragraph before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And here it says -- and I would like to read out, Mr. Groenewegen, a portion of this paragraph to remind you of the events. Thank you. "The BH Army, on the 21st of January, announced restrictions in the UN's freedom of movement in what is known as the Bandera Triangle after the BSA had taken up positions directly on the enclave boundary. The battalion," and here they're referring to your battalion, "decided to ignore the restrictions and entered the prohibited area with three patrols on the 27th of January. "This resulted in a response from the BH Army, who held approximately 100 DutchBat personnel hostage between 27 and 31st January. After this incident, the battalion no longer patrolled in the Bandera Triangle." My question for you is this, Mr. Groenewegen: Do you know anything about this document and this event? Do you have any personal knowledge of this event because you were in Srebrenica at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It is true I was in Srebrenica at the time, but I only heard that colleagues were taken hostage. I heard about that. But Bandera Triangle, I don't really know, and I wasn't present, myself, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will not dwell on this anymore, since you have no personal knowledge. Could you now tell us something else? On several occasions, you mentioned the theft of UN equipment during your stay in Srebrenica in 1995. Could you now please describe how this came about, and what measures did you then take once you established that some equipment had been stolen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: For the moment, I only remember one case where there was theft. It was a theft of petrol from OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us anything about that incident, and were Dutch soldiers involved in that theft or was the petrol actually taken by force? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It was during a period when one of my colleagues was standing watch, and several jerry cans of petrol were taken away. People broke into the place and took the jerry cans away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. Could you now tell me this: In the Popovic case, on page 2999 of the transcript, in response to Defence counsel's question, you said that the local people in Srebrenica pointed out that the local mafia headquarters was in Pale. Could you please confirm that here, and can you clarify that, because Pale is far away from Srebrenica, or was there some other Pale that they were actually referring to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, first, I don't remember ever saying that there was a headquarters -- mafia headquarters in Pale. I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But that is what is stated in transcript on page 2999 in the Popovic case. But thank you. Since you can't recall this, there is no need to dwell on it. Let's not waste any time. So my next question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It does not say that on that page, so I think it's unfair of him to be communicating this to the witness. It was in a question from one of the accused -- Defence lawyers about Pale, so I don't know what the purpose of that little misstatement was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir told us he doesn't want to dwell on this issue any longer. He can carry on. We have your intervention on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in response to what the Prosecutor said, I said in response to the question of one of the Defence counsel, you confirmed that the people of Srebrenica actually pointed out that the staff of the local mafia was in Pale, and I was just asking the witness if he can describe what Pale that is a reference to, because Pale is quite far from Srebrenica, and whether there was another place that they also called Pale. Thank you. Now I will move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mentioned here specifically the theft of petrol in jerry cans. How did the DutchBat safe-guard its equipment in order to prevent it from being stolen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: DutchBat has several locations, so I can only say what happened at OP Mike, where the theft took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm concerned with is only what measures were taken, so I will move on to another set of questions if you feel that there is no need for you to describe this theft. Can you tell us, please, when was it that the Muslims began arriving in Potocari? And if you feel that you want to describe the previous question -- that you want to answer it, you can also include it in the answer to this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. That is argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was really a set of different questions. Please break that up and put one question after the other. What is now your concrete question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I only had one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the witness confirm for us when it was that Muslim civilians began to arrive in the Potocari base in 1995? And then I just added to that that if the witness feels he wants to answer the previous question, he can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not necessary to repeat the whole part. I asked you to break up this whole part and you put one question to the witness, and there you should stop. Witness, you were asked to confirm when it was that Muslim civilians began to arrive at the Potocari base in 1995. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In earlier declarations, if I remember correctly, I quoted the date of July 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did these Muslim civilians arrive from their villages in the area to Potocari on UN vehicles, whether they picked them up en route, or whether they actually transported them there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, at first people reached us on foot. They arrived from the city of Srebrenica. And on one occasion, I saw a UN truck which was full of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did those first refugees who fled from Srebrenica and came to Potocari arrive on UN trucks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. Again, the first people I saw arriving in Potocari all came on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a few moments ago also -- in your reply, you said that they were also brought there on UN trucks. Is that correct or was the interpretation that I received incorrect?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. To be clear, a lot of people came in the direction of Potocari. I saw all of them on foot. And later on that day, I saw one truck that was filled with refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I seem to have a computer crash. It will take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we see it not recording any longer so that we must break and try to find out the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Would it be a good time to take the morning recess? I don't know how long it's going to take me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Tolimir, approaching the time for the first break. I think this is a convenient moment to resolve the technical problems. We adjourn now and will resume five minutes before 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope everything is working now with the record. Okay, very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just learned from Mr. Gajic that perhaps the plan is to continue with this witness for the rest of the day. If that's the case, we have a very sensitive witness waiting, and it would be nice if we could get an idea if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you give us some information about your indication?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I need a whole day for this witness, but I will use as much time as you give me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're saying you need the whole day. This is your right in cross-examination. But we don't want to find us in the position that all of a sudden the cross-examination has finished and there is still time available. But you are of the opinion that this will not happen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in the next two or three hours, I will finish, or maybe an hour before. If the Prosecutor needs that one hour at the end of the day, I will hurry up and finish within two hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does that help you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will be prepared, in any event. We have an investigator that can fill a gap, if there is a gap. This sensitive witness, I think, given what the general said, we would like to send him home, and we'll keep the investigator as the gap-filler potentially. We've informed the Defence that we have an investigator for just these reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That sounds very practical. At a later stage of our trial, and I hope we can clarify that quite soon, we will have more sitting days per week so that these problems are not so complicated. Thank you very much. Please carry on with your questioning, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, you have just told us that you saw a UN truck full of refugees. Could you please tell us what day was that when you saw that truck? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That must have been on 10 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the Army of Republika Srpska deployed in Potocari at that time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I hadn't seen them yet at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown 1D72, page 2 in English, the last paragraph, and page 3 in the Serbian, second paragraph. Thank you. Page 2, last paragraph, please look at it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am going to read for you: "On the 10th of July, 1995, around 1600 hours, Sergeant Van Schaik ordered us to leave the shelter. We were told to line up together with the infantry in order to escort the refugees who had started arriving at the base." Can we now turn to the following page in the English version, please. "I'm going to draw a green line to show where we stood. When I say 'refugees,' I mean Muslim refugees. At that moment, there were no BSA members at the compound in Potocari. "On that same day, from the direction of Bravo Company, four-ton UN trucks arrived. The trucks were packed with refugees, men, women, and children. In the course of one day, the compound filled up with refugees. According to my estimate, there were about 2.000 people there. Bravo Company was stationed in Srebrenica. "At one point, we could no longer cope with such an influx of refugees, and we had to hold the people back, to keep them off the compound. We allowed sick people to enter the base so that they could be attended to. We were up and about nearly the whole night." Thank you. This was a quote from your statement. I want you to say whether you remember that you stated that in your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I remember well that I stated that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 10th of July, did more refugees come to the compound where you were stationed? Did your superiors order you to receive them and accept them in the way you describe herein? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As it was described is the most accurate version of the course of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave it at that. Can we now talk about the Blagojevic/Jokic transcript page 1020. This is where you describe your duties and responsibility with regard to the refugees. And on line 7 and 8, you answer, and I quote: "... to make sure that people do not get lost and not to take the roads that were not intended for their use." My question is this: What roads were intended for them and what roads were banned for them? Can you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: There were no specifically prohibited roads, but from my perception, those in charge wanted to know where everybody was. That's why it was directed somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to your responsibilities at the base, and we're talking about the night between 11th and 12th on, page 1021, line 16 of the same transcript, you said, and I quote: "... to help people who sought our assistance." How did you assist them? What did the assistance consist of? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: At first, we had to determine whether people truly needed medical assistance or urgently needed other types of assistance, and that way we were able to triage the people according to urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, the Muslim civilians who gathered in Potocari, were they there in order to be transported to Tuzla, Sarajevo, and other areas under the control of the Muslim Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Blagojevic and Jokic case, when you talked about the evacuation on page 1025, you say the following, and I quote: "The first ones who left were those who wanted to get on the buses of their own will. Those who did not want to get on the buses withdrew, and they were then forced to get on the buses." Thank you, end of quote. My question is this: Why did you state that for the first time in the Blagojevic/Jokic case, despite the fact that you had had plenty of opportunities to talk about that even earlier, you had plenty of opportunities to say that some people had been forced to get on the buses? Thank you. To be very specific, you never made it part of your statements. You mentioned that for the first time in the Blagojevic/Jokic case and never before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: There are most likely other facts that were not mentioned, so please excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, did you personally, as a member of the Dutch Battalion in Potocari, help with the evacuations of those who had gathered in Potocari? Was that your official role or did you do it of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, our superiors told us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Did you ever hear from anybody, through an interpreter or personally, that some of the Muslims who had gathered in Potocari requested to stay in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the transcript, page 1026, the same case, Blagojevic and the other, you say on page 1026, lines 13 and 15, and I quote: "We talked to some of the people among the crowd, and they were convinced that they would be better off," and a reference here is to the Muslims, "to stay behind and to fight before they left voluntarily." My question is this: Were those your personal internal discussions or were those discussions conducted officially on the part of the representatives of the Dutch Battalion and the United Nations, whom you represented in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, such cases concerned personal discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us the day when such discussions were conducted? Was it on the 10th, the 11th, the 12th? Approximately, what day was that when you talked about that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did such discussion go on for all the three days or just one of the days? Could you give us some indication, in light of the fact that you spoke about that at the previous trial in which you testified? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It would probably have been one of those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your battalion command and you, yourself, know at the time that on the 11th, in the evening, the Muslims had already started breaking through towards Tuzla and that they invited all the others who didn't want to join them to make their way towards the UNPROFOR compound? Were you aware of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. We had the impression that things were happening, but that was the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor showed us a clip depicting your commander and representatives of the Muslims, who met on the 11th, in the evening, and the Muslims stated they were not in a position to inform their commanders that Mladic had proclaimed a cease-fire and that he invited them to come for talks on the following day, on the 12th. Did you know any of that? Were you aware of any of that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the negotiations in Bratunac which involved your commander, General Mladic, and Muslim representatives, thank you, on the 11th, in the evening, that actually it was your commander who had requested to meet with General Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: There again, I wasn't aware of that at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, for the transcript, when did you learn that your commander had requested to meet with General Mladic and to attend any negotiations between civilian representatives and the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, for me, I became aware of it much later, after the broadcast of the Dutch Battery -- sorry, after the deployment of the Dutch Battery.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 10th, when you saw the trucks that had arrived in Potocari, did you perhaps think that the Army of Republika Srpska was aware of the huge numbers of the civilians who had gathered in Potocari, and were you afraid that they might become a target for their artillery? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly had that thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In keeping with that, did you receive a task, an order from your superiors, from your commanders, from those who were in command?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As far as I reply, the only thing I remember is that we, as Blue Helmets, had to remain amongst the population so that we could be seen as being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that your personal choice, or your personal opinion, or wish, or estimate, or was that, rather, an order coming from your commander?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It was a combination of everything you just quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm going to show you something that you will certainly remember. In the Popovic case, on page 2967 of the transcript, you testified that your objective was to prevent conflicts between the two groups, the civilians, on the one side, and the RSK Army [as interpreted] on the other side. We're talking about the time when the RSK [as interpreted] arrived in Potocari. Could you please tell us when that was? When was the first time you noticed the presence of the Army of Republika Srpska in Potocari? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We just have just a slight correction. We need to make sure we've got the VRS. The RSK is the Republika Srpska Krajina, and they're not involved in this. We just need to get that translation correct. Thank you. I'm sure that wasn't in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see your agreement, Mr. Tolimir. Could it be perhaps helpful to have this portion of the testimony in Popovic on the screen to avoid any conflict about interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I accept this well-meant suggestion. I can't see the English -- I can't read the English transcript, and there's no Serbian transcript, so I have not checked that either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have page 2967 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have the 65 ter number of that document? No, you don't have. Okay. Then just carry on, but be always careful with the correct quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm just going to ask the witness whether he remembers that in that case he testified that it was their task to separate the civilians from the members of the Army of Republika Srpska when the troops of the Army of Republika Srpska arrived in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember that you stated that in the Popovic case? And that's the transcript that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, we have established that I didn't say anything that is not in the transcript. Thank you very much. And now I'll move on to another group of questions referring to the witness's statement, the one that he used here and confirmed that it's the same thing that he had previously stated in the Popovic case. Mr. Groenewegen, you have stated before this Trial Chamber and you mentioned a killing in your statement, the killing of a soldier by a house which you marked in a map that was shown to you by the OTP. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I do remember that, but I'm not sure your question was put quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement and in the transcript, we read about the killing of a soldier by a house where he was interviewed. Would that set the record straight? Is my question now more precise, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: In as far as I stated that, it's not the killing of a soldier. It's the killing of a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I accept your interpretation. Therefore, you're saying that he was a civilian. I suppose that you say that because he wore civilian clothes. But judging by his age, I suppose that he could have been a militarily able-bodied person. When you saw him, would that have been your opinion as well, just based on looking at him, his appearance and his age? Would you say that he was a militarily able-bodied man?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't think I am the one who has to judge on that, because anybody of that age could have been a military, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, was there anyone else with you when you eye-witnessed this event ?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, there was no one else from DutchBat next to me at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On this transcript, you said a little earlier that one of your assignments was to keep the civilians and the Republika Srpska Army soldiers separate, and then you said that you witnessed the killing of a civilian. Since it was your mandate to do what you described, can you tell us whether you have ever reported this incident, and to whom, and when?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: When you're referring to the incident, are you speaking of a report I should have made of this murder?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct. I was asking you about when it was that you reported this killing to your superior command because it was your mandate to keep the civilians separate from the soldiers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That evening, I reported for the first time on that incident, and that has been noted in the official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So there is an official document in respect of that. Now, in the Blagojevic case, on page 1036, lines 10 through 13, the Blagojevic/Jokic case, in response to the Prosecutor's question, and I quote his question: "Did you at any time have occasion to report what you had seen?" In reply to that, you said, I quote: "No, not on that same day." And then when you were asked when, on line 15, you said : "On the next morning." So which of the two is correct, what you've stated today or what you stated in the Blagojevic/Jokic case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Thank you to have freshened my memory. It is true that I only reported the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any reason for you to report that as late as the next morning because the incident involved a murder? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That is right. At that time, we were rather busy because there were so many refugees around us, and for that reason I did not think of reporting immediately, and that is why I only reported the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then tell us now whether any measures had been taken by the DutchBat organs to whom you reported that in your official capacity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I'm not certain I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked just a moment ago the following: Did your commander, or the competent officer to whom you reported the incident, take any measures regarding that incident? Did he inform the other party, the other side? Did he ask for any report as to what had happened? Thank you. Was there any measure taken? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that a report was made of -- minutes were taken of my report, I don't know whether any action was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I ask this is that those individuals who committed that criminal act were -- they could have abused their weapons, their position, their being in the army, so if it had been reported, then their superior officers could have taken appropriate measures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So then please tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- statements of reasons. That's not necessary. I would ask that he be required to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. You must not give a reason for a question. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have said this, and Mr. McCloskey actually interrupted me when I was framing my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What would the DutchBat -- or the unit that was there, what would they do on such an occasion if a DutchBat member committed that kind of criminal act? That was the gist and the drift of my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. This is not part of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just asking you about standard practice. But now let me ask you this: Did you have occasion to witness any instances of suicide during your mission in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Only the consequences of -- only the consequences of suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that on those critical days or did that occur earlier?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't really say when it happened. I remember I observed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot dwell on this any further because you can't remember the event, but let's move on to the next question. Was it your task to make a list of able-bodied men who arrived at the compound in the period between the 10th and the 12th, able-bodied men who arrived with a group of civilians?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, that was never one of my tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about that kind of task having been assigned to anyone in the compound?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness now please be shown document 1D1, debriefing of the Ministry of Defence of the Netherlands and Srebrenica -- correction, 1D16 -- or, rather, 1D74, page -- I apologise, I misspoke. The document is document 1D71, page 56, and the B/C/S version is page 74. Can we please see paragraphs 15 and 16 of this document, or, rather, 5.15 and 5.16. Thank you. I have it before me on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here: "Three refugees spoke for the others in the command. On the 13th of July, at the request of the battalion command, they drew up a list of 239 men of fighting age present on the compound, with the intention of submitting these later to the ICRS [as interpreted]. The battalion command hoped that the ICRS [as interpreted] would then be able to monitor these people and, if possible, to offer them some protection. At least 60 people refused to be registered. An attempt to make a similar list of refugees outside the compound failed, as both the refugee representatives and the interpreters were threatened (verbally)." In paragraph 6.25, only mention is made of that list being forwarded to the North-East Sector in The Hague by the DutchBat Command in Potocari. And it is also noted that the last refugees left the base on the 13th of July. Thank you. Has this helped jog your memory that there were attempts to compile such a list on the compound or around it by members of the civilian authorities or the Muslim authorities, and that your command had a problem with that because the people who had sought refuge on the compound actually opposed that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was never informed of the existence of such a list of persons. The only thing I can say is that the last persons left on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any representatives -- civilian representatives in your compound? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't have recognised them as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the debriefing of the Dutch Ministry of Defence, it says that refugees threatened soldiers and that 60 of them refused to be registered. Can you comment on that? What kind of threats were these, threats by Muslims to each other and also to the soldiers who tried to compile this list, thank you, in view of the fact that such a list was submitted by your commander to the superiors? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, I admit I don't remember any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it was not a correct quotation. In the report, it's only -- there's only written: "... as both the refugee representatives and the interpreters were threatened." There's nothing about who threatened them. You, in your question, you had a formulation that refugees threatened them. There's nothing in this report. I just wanted to state that for the sake of the record. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, do you know why interpreters had to get involved, in view of the fact that Muslim refugees and members of the commissions spoke the same language? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't really give an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, whether it is correct, as stated here in the debriefing, that the battalion command had actually submitted this report, this list, to the command at the Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. He doesn't know anything about this. I think he said this four or five times, at least. So this fishing expedition, while there's other witnesses, is really a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. This witness confirmed that he was interviewed by the Ministry of Defence in the Netherlands, and this debriefing was compiled based on those statements, and I only wanted to know whether the witness knew anything about this. And, Mr. President, if I stepped outside of the boundaries or the scope of the examination-in-chief, I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it was very clear that the witness couldn't give any answer and any opinion on that, so please carry on and not dwell on this any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you answer one question that I will put to you in relation to document 1D72? That is your statement. I would like the witness to be shown the penultimate page of that document, where you state, and I will quote a portion of your statement -- we will have it before us in a few moments. That's the penultimate page, the one before last. I quote: "From that day onwards, on the 12th of July, there was no more -- there were no more threats to the Dutch Battalion -- there was no longer any threat to DutchBat, and we could resume our normal duties at the compound and get our breath back." And now for my question. Can you tell us, please, what those normal duties at the compound were and why you could finally sigh a breath of relief?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Our normal activities were to -- were normal activities, but I can't really give details because I don't remember exactly what we did that day; probably make a list of the things we had, check where various people were, and we had to also clear a number of things out. And the fact that we got back -- our breath back, it means also that there were a number of things we needed to tell each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you cannot comment on that any further, I will move on to the next group of questions. Could the witness now please be shown document 1D47. These are proofing notes. 1D74. I apologise, I misspoke. So could we now please show the witness 1D74, briefing notes for this witness compiled on the 19th of October, 2006. I am not going to mention here the statements that you made for the press. I'm not really interested in that. I only have this question: The journalists who interviewed you, did they fairly report the information that you provided them, because the Prosecutor said that there were some errors in the report of what you had said to the reporters when your words were published in the press? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could he point out where the Prosecutor said there were errors? I don't recall that. I thought it was the witness that said there were errors, but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I wonder as well where this portion you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that. If Mr. McCloskey states that the witness actually said that, then the witness can probably tell us about it, because this was in his conversation with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So can the witness then tell us whether there were numerous errors in the press reports when his words were reported? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, some words were, indeed, distorted. And according to the press, things were said that I personally never said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document, 1D74, could we please have it on the screens, because I don't want the impression to be left here that I'm trying to conceal anything. Well, actually, we already have the document before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And in the document, we can read the following on the first page: "Before I step on a grass field, I think about it for a moment." And then it follows Mr. Groenewegen stated that the reporter got many of the details wrong or mixed up. In particular, he said that many of the things that were reported in the press, he had heard from Muslims, that he did not actually see them personally. He said that he had stated to the journalists that for the first group of Serb soldiers who arrived in the enclave, to him they appeared to be high on something, and that he never said that they were stiff with cocaine, as reported in the article. My question for the witness: Does it seem to you, because you had occasion to be misquoted by the journalists, that at times journalists were actually eager to report something even when it is misquoted, but very often at the expense of the Serbs, in this case, where you were saying something about Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: As for the reason why the press distorts things in an interview, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then just answer the following question, please. Before you stated this for the press, did you have to obtain approval from someone in the army, some command of the Dutch Army that was your superior command, because at the time you were a private? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I never received a press ban, so I never felt inhibited about saying anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What period does this statement apply to, as was conveyed by the journalists in your case here?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: This concerns the period from approximately 10 July through 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it customary for soldiers to use narcotics, drugs, and other such things in the Serbian Army and your army as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: In the Dutch Army, definitely not. As for the other case, I wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there another reason why the journalists portrayed the matter as they did? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please answer another question, and that question does not concern that particular subject.
